thread.title: Jana Partners Picks Up Facebook, Alphabet, Alibaba

author: Crystal Kim
title: Jana Partners Picks Up Facebook, Alphabet, Alibaba
text:
Mark Zuckerberg, CEO of Facebook Illustration: Ian Kennedy By Crystal Kim Aug. 14, 2018 3:20 p.m. ET While some investors were bailing on technology stocks, fearing a bubble could be forming , others were leaning in. Another season of so-called 13F portfolio disclosures, filings that give investors a peek into stock portfolios , shows that Jana Partners picked up new positions in social media giant Facebook (FB), Google parent Alphabet (GOOGL), and Chinese e-commerce juggernaut Alibaba Group Holding (BABA) in the second quarter.
The New York-based hedge fund bought more than 650,000 shares of Facebook, about 44,000 shares of Alphabet, and some 439,000 shares of Alibaba. It also added to its existing stake in Apple (AAPL). The firm could have changed its position in these stocks between the end of June and now—Facebook's shares were on a tear before turning radioactive late July—but their second-quarter conviction presents an interesting question to investors: to buy or not to buy tech.
Jana declined to comment on its tech-stock positions.
Hedge funds’ biggest gross long and short positions are both in the tech sector, according to Bank of America Merrill Lynch 's Savita Subramanian , based on the funds' aggregated reported long positions and estimated short positions. Yet large-cap active managers, in general, have reduced their relative weight in Facebook, Amazon.com (AMZN), Netflix (NFLX), and Alphabet from about a 70% overweight relative to the S&P two years ago to a 50% overweight now.
"But the crowding risks in FANG stocks and the tech sector still remain elevated, and the recent sell-off was likely a drag in fund performance in July," she writes.
Position matters because buying the most underweight stocks by large-cap active fund managers and selling the most overweight stocks by large-cap active funds has "consistently generated alpha," says Subramanian. She adds that the 10 most neglected stocks beat the 10 most crowded by an annualized spread of 90 percentage points on average in the first 15 days of every quarter since 2012.
One fun fact: Subramanian's screen for tech stocks with 20% or higher sales growth, long-term growth rates of 15% or higher, and market capitalizations of more than $65 billion yielded long-lost FANG brethren Adobe (ADBE) and Broadcom (AVGO).
Jana owns Adobe, which it first picked up in the first quarter of this year, but recent filings show that it has trimmed its position.
